title: From Reward-Free Representations to Preferences: Rethinking Offline Preference-Based Reinforcement Learning
claim: Prior methods first learn a reward or preference model then train the agent; ours pre-trains reward-free representations, then uses preferences to search and fine-tune.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right, (a)/(b) prior baselines versus (c) ours
description: Three side-by-side flow diagrams with captions (a) Reward modeling for PbRL, (b) Preference modeling for PbRL and (c) FB-PbRL (Ours). Each panel uses the same visual vocabulary. Blue cylinders are preference datasets, red/pink cylinders are unlabeled datasets, gray boxes are models, and yellow boxes are the agent π. In (a), the preference dataset trains a reward model by MLE. The reward model labels the unlabeled data, and offline RL then trains the agent. Panel (b) is similar, but a preference model feeds direct policy learning. Panel (c) is more complex. The unlabeled dataset feeds RFRL pre-training of Forward-Backward representations and a latent-conditional policy. The preference dataset drives contrastive search and fine-tuning, which yields a latent z* for the agent. The eye goes first to the repeated left-to-right chains, then to the denser panel (c).
caption: An illustration of the commonly used PbRL training pipelines and our proposed FB-PbRL framework.
abstract: Preference-based reinforcement learning (PbRL) avoids explicit reward engineering by learning from pairwise human preference feedback. Existing offline PbRL methods typically follow a two-stage pipeline, first learning a reward or preference model from labeled preferences and then performing offline RL on unlabeled data. We revisit offline PbRL through the lens of reward-free representation learning (RFRL) from the zero-shot RL literature, and propose a new training framework that first learns latent successor-measure representations from reward-free offline data, followed by contrastive search and fine-tuning using preference data. Through extensive experiments and ablations, we show that our method achieves superior preference efficiency over offline PbRL baselines. This work is the first to connect RFRL with PbRL, highlighting its potential as a feedback-efficient solution. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/rl-bandits-lab/FB-PbRL.
